passage: Flap, flap, flap. Four-year-old Gurpreet shuffled across the courtyard of their house near Bathinda in Papa's big leather chappals. He had Papa's old cloth bag over his shoulder, stuffed with folded newspaper. "Letter for Nirmala Dadi!" he shouted, just like Papa on his post round. He handed her a newspaper square. "Sign here, please. Jaldi." Dadi signed with her finger. Gurpreet puffed out his chest and flapped off to the buffalo shed with the next letter.

qa.q: Whose chappals was Gurpreet wearing?
qa.a: Papa's big leather chappals.

qa.q: Why does Gurpreet puff out his chest after delivering the 'letter'?
qa.a: Being like Papa makes him feel big and important, as if he has some of Papa's grown-up power.

qa.q: What did Dadi do that helped Gurpreet's game, and why is that a good choice?
qa.a: She played along and signed with her finger, which let him feel capable and admired in his pretend job.

qa.q: How might Papa feel if he came home and saw Gurpreet's post round?
qa.a: Probably touched and proud to see his son copying him so lovingly.

grounding: A four-year-old wears his father's chappals and copies his post round and phrases, feeling big like the adult he admires.

passage: In their flat in Melbourne, five-year-old Daniel clomped down the hallway in his dad's work clogs, which came up past his ankles. A toy stethoscope hung around his neck. "Hello, I'm Nurse Tuan," he told his teddy in a deep, calm voice. "This won't hurt. Deep breath for me. Good job, mate." His dad, Tuan, peeked around the door and heard his own words coming back at him. Daniel wrapped the teddy's paw in a sock bandage and patted it. "You're very brave. You can have a sticker."

qa.q: What did Daniel wear on his feet?
qa.a: His dad's work clogs.

qa.q: Why might copying his dad's words make Daniel feel good?
qa.a: Using his dad's calm nurse voice lets him feel big, kind and in charge, like the grown-up he admires.

qa.q: What could Tuan do next to support Daniel's game?
qa.a: Join in as a patient or give the teddy a real sticker, showing Daniel that his care is valued.

qa.q: What might it be like for Tuan to hear his own words coming back?
qa.a: Touching and a little funny, seeing how closely Daniel watches him and wants to be like him. 🙂

grounding: A five-year-old in Australia wears his father's work clogs and copies his nurse phrases, feeling big like the dad he admires.

passage: Five-year-old Vidya stood in the pretend-play corner of Little Stars Kindergarten wearing her mother's old flat sandals, the ones Amma had sent in for the dress-up box. She held a ruler like a pointer. "Good morning, class," she said to Raghav and three dolls. "Fingers on lips. Raghav, eyes on the board, please." It was exactly how Amma talked at her own school. Raghav giggled. Vidya didn't. She tapped the ruler, very serious. "We don't giggle during maths." The kindergarten teacher, watching, hid a smile.

qa.q: What did Vidya hold like a pointer?
qa.a: A ruler.

qa.q: Why does Vidya stay so serious when Raghav giggles?
qa.a: Being the teacher, like Amma, makes her feel proud, big and in charge, and she wants the game to feel real.

qa.q: How could the kindergarten teacher build on Vidya's play?
qa.a: Let her 'teach' a short counting song to the dolls, giving her a real chance to feel capable while keeping it fun.

qa.q: How might Raghav feel being told 'We don't giggle during maths'?
qa.a: Raghav might feel amused or a bit bossed about, and might want a turn being the teacher too.

grounding: A five-year-old in kindergarten wears her mother's sandals and copies her teacher phrases, feeling big like the parent she admires.

passage:
I'm Shalini, and I live below Lalremsiami's family in Aizawl. This morning I saw her, five years old, clomping along the landing in her Pa's big black boots, laces trailing. His old whistle hung round her neck. She stood in the middle of the stairs, held up one hand like Pa at the junction, and said in a deep voice, "Stop! Go slowly, please! No honking!" to three toy cars.
When I laughed, she didn't laugh back. She just stood straighter, very serious, as if the whole road depended on her.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami say to the three toy cars?
qa.a: "Stop! Go slowly, please! No honking!"

qa.q: Why might standing straighter in Pa's boots feel good to Lalremsiami?
qa.a: Being like Pa, who directs traffic at the junction, makes her feel big, important and safe, as if she has some of his strength.

qa.q: How could Shalini join in without spoiling the game?
qa.a: Shalini could take the play seriously, perhaps asking, "Officer, may I cross?", which respects Lalremsiami's pride instead of laughing.

qa.q: What might Pa feel if he saw his boots and whistle on the stairs?
qa.a: Pa would probably feel touched and proud to see Lalremsiami copying him so seriously 🙂

grounding: Shows a five-year-old clomping about in her father's boots and copying his traffic-police phrases, feeling big and safe by becoming like him.

passage:
Monday. Ankita, five, sat on a stool behind the glass at the bank while her mother, Jyoti, served the queue. "Next, please," Mummy said. "Sign here. Always count twice."
Wednesday. At home, Ankita shuffled about in Mummy's slippers, set up a stool behind the sofa, and cut paper into money. "Next, please!" she called to Nani. "Sign here, madam." She licked her thumb and counted, slowly.
Saturday. When the milkman came, Ankita ran to the door first, still in the slippers, holding the coins. "Wait," she told him, very grown-up. "Always count twice." Mummy laughed from the kitchen, and Ankita stood even taller.

qa.q: What did Ankita cut paper into?
qa.a: Money.

qa.q: Why does Ankita stand even taller when Mummy laughs from the kitchen?
qa.a: Being like Mummy at the bank makes her feel big and capable, and Mummy noticing makes her feel proud and safe 😊

qa.q: What small step could Mummy take to build on Ankita's game?
qa.a: Mummy could let Ankita help count real coins together at home, honouring the copying and teaching careful counting.

qa.q: How might the milkman see a five-year-old in big slippers saying "Always count twice"?
qa.a: He would probably find it charming and play along, seeing how seriously she copies her mother.

grounding: Illustrates a young child who wears her mother's slippers and copies her bank-counter phrases, feeling grown-up and safe by becoming like her.
